newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe inflation seen rising to around 24 pct.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe inflation seen rising to around 24 pct.

text.p: High money supply growth and expected hikes in excise duties are likely to push Zimbabwe's annual inflation rate up to around 24 percent in the last two quarters of the year, economic analysts said on Wednesday.
The consumer price index rose 21.4 percent year-on-year in June, up from 20.7 percent in May, largely boosted by increases in fuel prices.
"We are going to see inflation moving up sharply in the third and fourth quarters, to about 24 percent," said Anthony Hawkins, business lecturer at Harare's University of Zimbabwe.
"It's going to be difficult to bring it down now. Money supply is growing at a tremendous rate. It's been above 30 percent for a long time..." he told Reuters.
Broadly-defined yearly money supply growth is currently at 33.8 percent.
Hawkins and Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe chief economist Danny Dube said money supply growth was being driven largely by the government's budget deficit.
This is expected to increase to 10.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the fiscal year ended June 30, well above the target of 8.5 percent.
They said recent wage settlements would also put the government under pressure to raise the money to award civil servants pay hikes of 30 percent which it had promised.

Dube and Hawkins said the government -- under pressure from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund to trim the deficit -- was likely to raise a number of taxes as well as alcohol and cigarette prices in the budget to be presented next Thursday to increase its revenues.
The budget would run for 18 months to December 1998 as the government moves to a calendar year from the traditional July to June year.
Private economic consultant John Robertson said much would depend on planned government spending in the coming budget.

"A lot of government spending is very inflationary ... They spend what they have on paying staff and not on getting things like infrastructure fixed. This is causing a fall in profitability in the productive sector," he said.
Government spending -- largely to meet its wage bill -- accounts for 40 percent of GDP.
